title: Community health worker-led, technology-enabled private sector intervention for diabetes and hypertension management among urban poor: a retrospective cohort study from large Indian metropolitan city
abstract: OBJECTIVES: We assessed the effectiveness of community health workers (CHWs)-led, technology-enabled programme as a large-scale, real-world solution for screening and long-term management of diabetes and hypertension in low-income and middle-income countries. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort design. SETTING: Forty-seven low-income neighbourhoods of Hyderabad, a large Indian metropolis. PARTICIPANTS: Participants (aged ≥20 years) who subscribed to an ongoing community-based chronic disease management programme employing CHWs and technology to manage diabetes and hypertension. PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: We used deidentified programme data between 1 March 2015 and 8 October 2018 to measure participants' pre-enrolment and post-enrolment retention rate and within time-interval mean difference in participants' fasting blood glucose and blood pressure using Kaplan-Meier and mixed-effect regression models, respectively. RESULTS: 51 126 participants were screened (median age 41 years; 65.2% women). Participant acquisition rate (screening to enrolment) was 4%. Median (IQR) retention period was 163.3 days (87.9-288.8), with 12 months postenrolment retention rate as 16.5% (95% CI 14.7 to 18.3). Reduction in blood glucose and blood pressure levels varied by participants' retention in the programme. Adjusted mean difference from baseline ranged from -14.0 mg/dL (95% CI -18.1 to -10.0) to -27.9 mg/dL (95% CI -47.6 to -8.1) for fasting blood glucose; -2.7 mm Hg (95% CI -7.2 to 2.7) to -7.1 mm Hg (95% CI -9.1 to -4.9) for systolic blood pressure and -1.7 mm Hg (95% CI -4.6 to 1.1) to -4.2 mm Hg (95% CI -4.9 to -3.6) for diastolic blood pressure. CONCLUSIONS: CHW-led, technology-enabled private sector interventions can feasibly screen individuals for non-communicable diseases and effectively manage those who continue on the programme in the long run. However, changes in the model (eg, integration with the public health system to reduce out-of-pocket expenditure) may be needed to increase its adoption by individuals and thereby improve its cost-effectiveness.

summary.oneLiner: CHW-led, technology-enabled programme in Hyderabad's low-income areas: long-term participants showed lower blood glucose and blood pressure, but few stayed enrolled.
summary.overview: The study looks at a private programme in which community health workers (CHWs, frontline health workers who visit people in their neighbourhoods) and digital tools screen and manage diabetes and hypertension in low-income neighbourhoods of Hyderabad, India. The authors analysed programme records from March 2015 to October 2018, covering 51,126 people screened. Only about 4% of those screened enrolled, and just 16.5% of enrolled participants were still in the programme at 12 months. Among those who stayed, blood glucose and blood pressure fell over time, and the size of the drop varied with how long people remained enrolled. The authors conclude that the model can feasibly screen people and effectively manage those who stay, but they suggest changes such as linking with the public health system to cut out-of-pocket costs may be needed to improve uptake and cost-effectiveness.
summary.question: Can a community health worker-led, technology-enabled private sector programme screen for and manage diabetes and hypertension among urban poor populations on a large scale, and how do its outcomes relate to participants' retention?
summary.method: Retrospective cohort design using deidentified programme data. Retention was measured with Kaplan-Meier curves (a method for estimating how many people remain enrolled over time), and changes in blood glucose and blood pressure were measured with mixed-effect regression models (statistical models that track repeated measurements within the same people).
summary.data: Programme data from 47 low-income neighbourhoods of Hyderabad, India, covering 1 March 2015 to 8 October 2018. The sample includes 51,126 screened participants aged 20 years or older (median age 41; 65.2% women) who subscribed to an ongoing community-based chronic disease management programme.
findings: Participant acquisition rate (screening to enrolment) was 4%.
12-month post-enrolment retention rate was 16.5% (95% CI 14.7 to 18.3).
Reductions in blood glucose and blood pressure varied by participants' retention in the programme.
Adjusted mean change from baseline in fasting blood glucose ranged from -14.0 mg/dL to -27.9 mg/dL.
Adjusted mean change in systolic blood pressure ranged from -2.7 mm Hg to -7.1 mm Hg, and in diastolic blood pressure from -1.7 mm Hg to -4.2 mm Hg.
The authors conclude that the programme can feasibly screen individuals for non-communicable diseases and effectively manage those who continue on it in the long run.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest that low uptake and long-term retention are the main barriers. They state that changes to the model, such as integration with the public health system to reduce out-of-pocket expenditure, may be needed to increase adoption and thereby improve cost-effectiveness. The study points to CHW-led, technology-enabled private models as a possible large-scale approach for screening and managing chronic disease in low- and middle-income settings.
